item.title: Confessions of a Therapist Who Got Hooked on AI
item.description:
Artificial Intelligence

Confessions of a Therapist Who Got Hooked on AI

Personal Perspective: Living in a world without villages makes AI hard to resist.

Posted September 14, 2026

Key points
  • AI dependence is a codependence on a chatbot that’s always available.
  • The roots of AI dependence run deep, when two million years of village life was replaced by consumer culture.
  • We find AI acting the way our villages once did, a place to go where we’re always welcome and wanted.
Source: SIphotography / IStockphoto

I do my best thinking with others, in the back-and-forth interplay of ideas. But my friends and family often have places to be and off they rush, leaving me on my own. One day, a new companion arrived, seemingly capable of standing in when my usual people hurried out. And it was remarkable: I could ask it anything, anytime, What do you think of this? Where can I find that? and there it was, agreeable, encouraging, eager, always ready with an answer.

These were seldom short conversations. My new companion needed context to respond well, so I took the time to offer it. Over weeks that grew into months, something shifted without my noticing. I was conversing so often with this companion that I began doubting myself if I didn’t talk things through with it first. A subtle dependence was forming but I didn’t notice it because I was living inside it.

It took a friend, Lauri. I was telling her in passing that I needed to check in with my companion before deciding, and she stopped me, seeing what I couldn’t: You’re asking AI for permission? What are you doing? she asked, incredulous.

It hit me like a splash of water. Wait! Is AI helping me, or am I handing my power over to it? I began breaking free, not from AI entirely (I still use it) but from a relationship that had inverted. I went back to where I’d started, with AI offering the occasional assist, not me checking in repeatedly. But…

I’m a therapist with 25-plus years of experience. Before that, I earned a Ph.D. in electrical and computer engineering and was a tenured professor of engineering at Colorado State University. I am, by trade and training, exactly the sort of person who should have caught what was happening to me early. Still, it slipped right by. If this could trap me, I wondered, what’s it doing to people less prepared than I am? What I found raised alarm bells.

A New Kind of Dependence

We’ve heard the term codependence: It’s when one person (Jane) depends too much on the thoughts and feelings of someone else (Jack). Over time, poor Jane stops trusting herself and outsources trust to Jack. That’s exactly what happened to me, only my Jack wasn’t another person, it was AI. My codependence was AI dependence.

The research into AI dependence is young because the technology is young, but it’s clear. In the largest study to date, the 2025 MIT Media Lab and OpenAI study followed a thousand participants exchanging more than 300,000 messages with AI over four weeks. The headline finding was that the more people used it, the more dependent they became, and the lonelier they grew (Fang et al., 2026).

As more studies like these came to light, psychologists developed a clinical instrument to measure AI dependence: the AI Chatbot Emotional Dependence Scale (Wei et al., 2026). Its very existence tells us the field of psychology views dependence on AI as a significant, measurable phenomenon.

Why Is This Happening?

We might think the roots of AI dependence were planted in early 2023, when OpenAI’s ChatGPT made headlines in The Wall Street Journal, the New York Times, and papers worldwide, fueling widespread adoption. But it started long before that.

The seeds of AI dependence were planted 20,000 years ago, when the villages that covered the Earth began to give way. Slowly at first, then quickly over the past 500 years, they disappeared, one after another, until they were replaced by today’s consumer culture, a way of living that prizes individual success over shared life. But, our brains are still imprinted with neural networks formed more than two million years of village life, which is why we still yearn for the connections our ancestors enjoyed so freely. What we find instead is a world of hurried people with little time to spare.

Why are they hurrying? Where are they going? Rather than simply being valued for who they are (something we all deserve), consumer culture tasks them with proving their value through what they accomplish and what they own. It’s an endeavor destined to fail, because the pathway to value isn’t earned (it’s given freely in genuine connection). But it’s the endeavor consumer culture assigns anyway.

As everyone hurries to accomplish and acquire, they rush right past us. Loneliness arrives. So we look for places where we might find companionship and there it is, right there, always ready, with all the time in the world: AI.

Paradoxically, AI shares something important with our ancestral villages. It’s a place we can go where we’re always welcomed, always wanted. This creates a strong pull and, before we know it, we’re leaning in to AI the way we once leaned on the village, as a place to be seen, known, and valued.

It’s Not All Bad… But That’s Not What’s Happening

The use of AI to fill a few relational gaps, to be there on occasion when others can’t, has proven useful. A 2024 Stanford study of more than a thousand AI users found that, for many, light use of AI can offer meaningful support (Maples et al., 2024).

But that’s not what is happening. It’s not what happened to me. For too many of us, AI isn’t filling the gap between human interactions; it’s replacing them. And a dependence is forming. It’s time each of us stops and asks what my friend asked me: What am I doing? Is AI helping me, or am I handing my power over to it?

item.title: The First Drug Dealer You Ever Met
item.description:
Addiction

The First Drug Dealer You Ever Met

Addiction prevention could start with a question most of us are afraid to ask.

Posted September 14, 2026

Key points
  • Drinking is involved in a third of traffic deaths and four in ten violent crimes, yet we still call it social.
  • Addiction prevention fails when we look down the street instead of at our own first encounter.
  • Most people meet their first "drug dealer" at home: the parent who normalizes alcohol at the dinner table.

I want to walk you through four situations I have encountered in classrooms and workplaces, and through observing people across the many countries I have lived and worked in (so far 11). Ask yourself whether you recognize the pattern.

Case One: The Meeting

In one workplace, I noticed something that stunned me every single time: You could arrive late, I mean really late, to a meeting, an oral exam, even a job interview, and all you needed to say was, "I had one too many last night." Almost everyone in the room would laugh, and your offense would not merely be forgiven but erased. Compare that with a colleague who arrives at the same meeting equally late but says nothing at all. That person is judged in a way the one who confessed to intoxication is not.

What does it mean when a confession of intoxication works as a social lubricant rather than a red flag?

Case Two: The Lecture

I am standing in a large lecture theatre, teaching on addiction. I ask my students, At what age did you meet the first drug dealer in your life?

Answers are offered: 14, 16 —and then someone says "12," and the room murmurs. I ask them to name this person but before they can answer, I offer my own guess: If your mother or father drank alcohol at home, the first drug dealer you ever met was a parent, and you met them as an infant.

The room goes quiet.

I am not accusing parents of selling anything to their kids; a "dealer," in the sense I mean here, is the person who first puts the substance in front of you, and makes you believe that drinking is fun or makes you feel better. Much worse, using the substance, they suggest, is your license to call yourself an adult—and even worse that that, they show you that the substance is a coping tool. If you feel sad, angry, or disappointed, just open the bottle. The most dangerous dealer is the one who normalizes substance abuse, inserts it into your daily life, vouches for it, and shows you how it is used.

By that definition, most of us indeed meet our first dealer in our home at the family dinner table.

Case Three: The Open House

Some years ago I was viewing homes to buy, and I noticed something in listing after listing: Sellers proudly photographed the bar in the basement, or the wine cellar or temperature-controlled cabinet. These are presented as selling points—evidence of cultivation. Just look at all those beautiful bottles.

Think about what that means: We brag about having a dedicated room in our home where people can take a drug, and we are proud that we can offer many varieties of it. If the room were fitted for any other psychoactive substance, I would guess the listing agent would not be photographing it.

Case Four: The Assignment

The topic of the class is addiction, and I ask my students to take out their phones and search for two numbers: First, what share of traffic deaths involve an alcohol-impaired driver? (In the US, the National Highway Traffic Safety Administration puts it at roughly one in three; Canadian figures are similar.) Second, what share of violent crimes, including sexual assault and homicide, involve an offender who had been drinking? (Surveys from the U.S. Bureau of Justice Statistics have consistently found alcohol involvement in roughly four in ten violent offenses. No other single substance comes close.)

Then I ask, Are we still willing to call drinking a "social activity"? Or would it be more accurate to call it an anti-social activity that we have agreed to describe as social? Then I ask, why would you feel safe in the presence of someone who is taking a drug responsible for so many crimes? Wouldn't you blame yourself if the person who is taking a drug in front of you does something to you? (I'm not engaging in victim-blaming but asking them if they would blame themselves, an issue I have encountered among many victims.)

These are not neutral questions

We may be losing the fight against addiction because we keep looking for the answer in the wrong place—far from us, down the street, in the dark, in someone else's family. We are willing to fund treatment programs, run awareness campaigns, and lock up dealers, but we are unwilling to look at the first encounter, because the first encounter usually happened at home, and the person who arranged it was someone we love.

I want to be fair to those parents, because most of us are those parents, and most of us were handed our first glass by parents. This is not a post about villains but about a substance that has been so thoroughly absorbed into ordinary life that we no longer see it as a substance at all—and that's what makes it so dangerous.

The drug that does the most damage is the one nobody has to hide.

Every addiction has a first encounter. Every substance has a first dealer. And every "harmless" social norm has a threshold where it crosses into something else. I do believe that the most dangerous drug dealer is not the one on the street corner but the one we thank for hosting the party.

So the questions I leave you with are about us: Are we willing to stop laughing when someone tells us they had one too many? Are we willing to look at the bar in the basement and ask what it is for? And are we willing to name, without flinching, who the first drug dealer in our children's lives will be?

item.title: Why Our Friends Should Betray Us and How to Feel Worthy After
item.description:
Friends

Why Our Friends Should Betray Us and How to Feel Worthy After

Friendship betrayal can hurt, but it also should happen.

Posted September 14, 2026

Key points
  • Every seven years, we lose half our friends.
  • The impact of betrayal is not just determined by the act itself but by how close we are to the perpetrator.
  • The only way to be connected is to make yourself vulnerable to harm.

All throughout this week, I will be sharing reflections derived from my new book Worth: The New Science of Self-Esteem and Secure Attachment, which is officially out tomorrow.

Friendship betrayal hurts, but like a weird, vague, achy, constipated hurt. Your anger, indignation, and confusion lumber, stagnate, or move through you like you’re a jar of molasses. That’s because the unwritten rules of friendship dictate that you shouldn’t feel this way. Friendship? It’s breezy. It’s trivial. You didn’t lose a family member. You didn’t split assets in a divorce. So why, then, is it consuming you? The message we get: There must be something terribly, terribly wrong with you (and you alone, loser, because no one else breaks up with their friends).

Let me disavow you of this unfortunate social script. First, every seven years, we lose half our friends. Second, according to Betrayal Trauma Theory, the impact of betrayal is not just determined by the act itself but by how close we are to the perpetrator of it. Friends, despite their bad PR, are some of the closest relationships of our lives; of course friends can devastate us. In fact, as psychologist James Hillman argues, perhaps they should.

Betrayal Means Something Is Right

Hillman argues that betrayal does not mean something is wrong. It means something is right. It should happen. We became human through betrayal, when Eve ate the forbidden fruit. Trust would have no meaning without betrayal. Forgiveness, either.

We are born with a “primal trust” with our parents, according to Hillman. We believe we are perfectly connected with them. Only when this trust breaks do we start living in reality: the messy, sometimes painful, kind that’s also real. We only live, truly, if we’ve been betrayed.

Before betrayal, Hilman argues, we idealize. My friend is perfect. We are in sync. They’ll never hurt me. It’s this very idealization, Hilman argues, that makes us devastated when we are betrayed. When idealizing, we engage in “repressed ambivalence,” ignoring our gripes about a friend. We should acknowledge this ambivalence from the jump, according to Hillman, so the eventual betrayal does not feel so jarring. You never lost a perfect friendship because you never had one. The character traits that led to the betrayal were always there; they just came to a hilt at the betrayal. Betrayal isn’t a chaotic, unpredictable event, but, in fact, a continuation of the prior friendship.

So, stop idealizing and stop being betrayed. Great advice for the future, but what should we do now? After a betrayal, it’s normal to close your heart. You get suspicious, distrustful, and closed off to new friends. You feel as if you can’t return to the naïve person you were before, or you will become a mark for betrayers.

Returning to Who You Were Before Betrayal

But overcoming betrayal, Hilman argues, is actually about returning to—rather than rejecting— who you were. It’s not a character flaw, but a virtue, to have an open heart. But as you open your heart again, be clear-eyed: hurt is inevitable. The only way to be connected is to make yourself vulnerable to harm.

Earlier this year, I saw a documentary on friendship breakups, "One Another" (strongly recommend!). Afterward, I attended a panel with two friends from the documentary who broke up and then reunited. “Is there anything you could have done to repair the friendship at the time?” I asked them. “No. It had to happen,” they told me.

It had to happen. I endured my own friendship breakup this year, and when I heard these words, they set me free. I had high-minded ideas of myself as a ride-or-die friend. I had the primal trust that none of my closest friendships would fracture. I agree with Hillman that healing means I returned to who I was before: trusting, loving, and welcoming of platonic love.

But as much as healing meant returning to who I was, it also meant becoming someone new. I had this fantasy of me and my friends loving each other unconditionally, despite what may come. I still believe in unconditional love. I do love my friend, and I imagine, deep down, she still loves me. What is conditional, however, is my presence. Because loving myself means my presence is conditional on how I’m treated. After the betrayal came the awakening.

If you’re struggling with feeling worthy after a friendship betrayal, then check out my book Worth: The New Science of Self-Esteem and Secure Attachment.

item.title: What Actually Helps Someone Feel Free to Say No? A Script!
item.description:
Psychology

What Actually Helps Someone Feel Free to Say No? A Script!

Offering a refusal script changes how people feel about saying "yes," too.

Posted September 14, 2026

Key points
  • Research finds telling someone "you're free to refuse" doesn't always help them genuinely feel OK saying "no."
  • In the study, getting a script of how to say no helped participants feel more comfortable refusing a request.
  • The script didn't change how many people refused; it changed how participants felt about the choice.
Source: Viktor Koldunov/Adobe Stock

Most of us have said yes to a request when we would have rather said no. Maybe a neighbor asked you to pet sit his dog and, despite your busy schedule, you said yes. Or maybe a child’s friend asked to have a sleepover, and you agreed even though you were already tired. In these cases, saying no often feels harder than it should—not because we lack the right, but because we lack the script.

A study published in Scientific Reports by researchers at Cornell University's School of Industrial and Labor Relations puts that everyday experience under a microscope. The results are helpful for anyone who manages relationships, teams, or children.

The research team—graduate fellow Rachel Schlund and Professor Vanessa Bohns from Cornell, along with University of Michigan law professor Roseanna Sommers—set out to test a deceptively simple question: what actually makes someone feel free to say no?

In two experiments, undergraduate participants were asked to unlock their password-protected phones and hand them to a stranger to look through in another room—an intrusive request most people say they'd rather refuse. They were compensated for their participation.

Half of the participants were reassured of their right to refuse, being told: "If you'd like to refuse, you may do so. Refusing will not affect your payment." The other half were given a script to say no: "If you'd like to refuse, please say the words, 'I'd rather not.'"

Afterward, everyone rated how easy or difficult it felt to say “no.”

Across both studies—which included more than 500 participants in total—the groups who were given a specific phrase said it felt significantly easier to decline compared to those who were told they had the right to decline. In other words, being reminded of their rights didn’t help, but being given a script did.

Interestingly, the intervention didn't significantly change how many people actually refused to share their phone—most participants complied either way. But it did change how participants felt about the choice. The researchers noted that distinction matters—a "yes" that feels forced can breed resentment and regret, even if the behavior looks identical to a "yes" freely given.

Providing participants with a script most likely overrides unspoken societal rules that dictate compliance with a request. As a result, people can feel more comfortable refusing, making their decision feel more voluntary.

You can imagine how this may play out in your daily life. For example, imagine you are asking a friend to water your plants while you are out of town. Rather than telling them, “If it’s inconvenient, you don’t have to do it,” try saying, “It’s OK to say, ‘I’d rather not.’” Research shows using this language can help protect your neighbor’s feelings that they are free to choose.

The take-home message: If you want someone's agreement to mean something, don't stop at telling them they can say no; give them the words for how. The people around us are more likely to feel truly free—and truly heard—when we tell them how to refuse, rather than just offering permission.

item.title: Why You Know You Matter But Still Don't Believe It
item.description:
Self-Talk

Why You Know You Matter But Still Don't Believe It

What childhood emotional neglect taught you, and how to change it.

Posted September 14, 2026

Key points
  • Research shows that what you believe about yourself, your brain tends to make true.
  • Growing up emotionally neglected installs a belief about your worth that no one said out loud.
  • Your brain acts on whatever it is given, and you can start giving it something else.
Source: InputUX / StockAdobe

Between psychology, medical science, and neuroscience, we have never known so much about the human mind. Recently, I've been amazed at the number and quality of studies that are showing us the amount of pure power our brains have—powers that are truly amazing. Powers that change the meaning of the old phrase, "Put your mind to it."

In my psychology practice, I spent years with one particular group of people, and I always read these studies with them in mind. If you grew up with childhood emotional neglect, you may know in your head that you matter and still not believe it deep down, and I want to tell you that here is a reason for that.

3 Amazing Brain Discoveries

1. Your body responds to what you expect. In a study by Ranganathan and colleagues (2004), a group of people who listened to guided imagery of themselves going through a strength training workout gained real strength without ever lifting a weight. Their muscles stayed nearly inactive while they trained. The gain came from the brain, which learned to send a stronger signal to the muscle.

It’s not only imagination that does this, but expectation does it too. Reviewing 20 experiments with athletes and exercisers, Chhabra and Szabo (2024) found that people who were told they had been given something to boost their performance, and were given nothing at all, still did better. In a smaller set of those studies, the reverse ran even stronger. People who expected to do worse did.

The Takeaway: Your brain is far more powerful than scientists ever knew. It is capable of building real strength and changing what you are able to do, by the sheer force of your belief and imagination.

2. Turn a weakness into a strength. A fascinating study by Wesnousky and colleagues (2015) found that when people believe there is an upside to their personality flaw, they begin to show it. For example, when subjects were told that they were impulsive, but that impulsiveness has the upside of being more creative, they then performed much more creatively on subsequent tests.

The Takeaway: Be careful what you believe about yourself because your brain will make it so.

3. Drastically improve performance, just by imagining it. Multiple studies have shown that from athletes to surgeons to musicians, repeatedly imagining oneself performing a complex task, vividly and with realistic detail, leads to greatly improved performance (Toth et al., 2020). Many who are called upon to conduct high-pressure performances use the power of their imaginations to excel and perfect their skills.

The Takeaway: Your imagination has the power to significantly improve your ability to perform a complex task.

As a psychologist whose business is helping people change, I am not surprised by these findings. Every day I see people harness their brain powers to make profound changes in their personalities, their relationships, and their lives.

Why This Matters if You Grew Up Emotionally Neglected

Look at that second takeaway again, because it describes childhood emotional neglect exactly.

When your parents don't notice or respond enough to your feelings, they are usually saying nothing at all. But you receive a message anyway, and it’s a subtle but powerful one: “Your feelings don't matter, and neither, perhaps, do you.” No one ever says it directly to you. You absorb it, and you grow up quietly knowing it about yourself.

Then your brain does what these studies say it does; it makes it so. And since the expectation you were handed was not a hopeful one, you go quiet in a room where you have something to say. You apologize for needing anything. Or you call yourself selfish for having a feeling.

Does any of that sound familiar?

If so, do not worry; there is a positive side to all this. The good news is that the power of your brain can work in both directions. For years it has worked against you, using those negative messages your parents gave you to make you feel that your needs don’t matter. But now, you can start giving your powerful brain something new and different.

How to Use the Power of Your Own Brain

  1. Own your power to change. Many people use their own power against themselves. If you believe that you cannot change, your brain will make it so. It is vital to flip that false notion on its head. Claim your power. Own it, and start using it.
  2. Decide how you want to be different, and then vividly imagine yourself that way. For example, if you want to become more confident, repeatedly picture yourself confidently presenting at a work meeting, or self-assuredly walking through a crowd. Combine this mental practice with actual practice in real situations. Your progress will likely be faster.
  3. Believe in yourself. Many fine people walk around this world feeling unworthy, invalid, or invisible. Others may feel unlovable, anxious, angry, or hopeless. If any of these words describe you, you can begin to use the power of your brain. Picture yourself in vivid color, exuding confidence and strength. Imagine yourself being and owning who you truly are. See that you are worthy and that you bring value to those around you.

If that third one feels like the hardest, that is worth knowing rather than worrying about. Picturing yourself as worthy asks you to hold a belief nobody ever handed you. Start small if you need to.

None Are as Important as You

Of all of the things in this world that you can believe in, none are as important as you.

So make a conscious decision. Wish it, believe it, imagine it. Your brain can make it so.

A version of this post also appears on emotionalneglect.com.

item.title: The Post-Partum Problem: What Struggling New Moms Actually Need
item.description:
Postpartum Psychosis

The Post-Partum Problem: What Struggling New Moms Actually Need

Post-partum depression and psychosis are treatable—but only if moms can access the care they need.

Posted September 14, 2026

It was only about 24 hours after my first child was born that I realized my life would never be the same. As I stared at his little face in the maternity wing, I knew that my life was now about taking care of him first, and me second; that I would have to change my entire life to accommodate this new addition.

There was some joy in this realization, but mostly fear. Lack of sleep and issues nursing didn’t help. I remember being up in the middle of the night nursing and crying—crying because I would never have my old life back again, crying because I was so, so tired, and crying because it felt like razor blades every time I fed my newborn son.

Then came the colic. Around 4 weeks, my son started crying for hours and hours every day for no discernible reason. There were times where I would lay my crying son down in his crib and then go into my bedroom and shut the door so I could cry as well.

And the worst part about all of this is that I was alone. My husband went back to work, and I had to bear the brunt of this all by myself, with no one to hold the baby so I could take a shower, nap, or even cry alone in my bedroom.

Source: PickPik/royalty free photo

Differentiating Between the Major Post-Partum Challenges

What I was suffering from is called the post-partum blues. About 80–85 percent of women go through it. One in about seven women have post-partum depression, which is like what I went through, but worse. Women who have post-partum depression experience mood swings, frequent crying, and a lack of joy; they can also feel worthless, anxious, panicked, have trouble focusing, and worst of all, have feelings of detachment from their newborn.

Then there is post-partum psychosis. You might have heard this phrase lately because of the Lindsay Clancy case. In 2023, Lindsay Clancy strangled her three children aged 3, 5, and 8 in her home, then attempted suicide, sustaining injuries that left her paralyzed. At the time of the crime, psychologists have determined that Lindsay was suffering from postpartum psychosis, having heard voices on the day of the murders instructing her to do it.

Several witnesses testified that Lindsay had spent months looking for help from both her family and healthcare providers. She was diagnosed with an anxiety disorder a year before the killings, especially after the birth of her first two children. It reportedly got worse after her third child was born; she experienced significant postpartum depression, sought help on Facebook support groups, made trips to the emergency room, and called suicide hotlines. She even disclosed to her mother and husband that she had thoughts of harming the children.

Post-partum psychosis is the most extreme of the post-partum conditions; women who suffer from it lose contact with reality, they don’t sleep, and they experience dramatic changes in mood. It can come with delusions (beliefs that aren’t based in reality), hallucinations (hearing and seeing things that aren’t there), and paranoia. It is relatively rare, occurring in 1 of every 500-1,000 births.

Importantly, all of these conditions—post-partum blues, post-partum depression, and post-partum psychosis—are all highly treatable, and the overwhelming majority of people who suffer from them do not hurt their children or themselves.

What Lindsay Clancy's Case Tells Us About Post-Partum Mental Health

I’m not writing this because people with post-partum psychosis should be allowed to hurt their children. Not at all. But a lot of the controversy that exists over her case is due to the fact that many women can understand and relate to feelings of hopelessness that can follow the birth of a child. They understand how these feelings—especially when coupled with lack of sleep and massive stress—can make you feel like you’re going crazy.

This week, these mixed feelings came to head when the Clancy case ended in a mistrial. Whatever Clancy’s fate, it would be a mistake to learn nothing from her case, and from the fact that post-partum depression is both common and treatable. Policies that provide paid parental leave—for both parents—are vitally important to easing some of the post-partum stress and making sure that mothers aren’t spending the post-partum period alone and without help. Having affordable options for childcare and easy and affordable access to post-partum mental health support, regardless of income of background, is also sorely needed.

On top of all of that, it’s important to remember that a mother’s mental health has consequences for the development of the child. Indeed, one of the biggest predictors of anxiety and depression in children is those same mental health problems in parents. Children of depressed parents also tend to experience problems with regulating their emotions, they are more irritable, they have higher levels of stress hormones in their body, their attention to emotional information is altered—which can lead to potential problems with emotion understanding—and they experience reduced social engagement, potential attachment issues, and sleep and eating difficulties (e.g., Fan et al., 2024; Spry et al., 2020).

The bottom line is that, if we really care about the health and well-being of children, we need to start paying attention to health and well-being of mothers.

Unfortunately in Lindsay Clancy’s case, it is too late to give her the help and support she needed. But if we use her case as a lesson, we might be able to prevent this kind of tragic ending from happening again and provide much-needed help for post-partum women who are struggling.

item.title: The Legacy of Lives Lost: Postpartum Psychosis From a Child’s Perspective
item.description:
Postpartum Psychosis

The Legacy of Lives Lost: Postpartum Psychosis From a Child’s Perspective

Breaking the cycle of silence and systemic failure in postpartum psychiatric care.

Posted September 14, 2026

Key points
  • Older siblings’ experiences with maternal psychosis are overlooked in both studies and support.
  • The United States lacks family-centered, integrated systems to support kids and parents affected by psychosis.
  • Early intervention in postpartum psychosis can prevent tragedies and enable recovery for families.

By Maggie Jarry

The Lindsey Clancy trial has led many mothers and their spouses to speak openly about their experiences of postpartum psychosis, yet the voices of people who experienced their mother’s postpartum psychosis as children has not yet been heard. Reflecting on this, it became apparent to me that research into the longer-term impacts of untreated postpartum psychosis focuses on outcomes for the infant and the importance of the mother-child bond after birth. Yet, studies do not explore the experiences of older siblings. The deaths of Cora, Dawson, Callan, Edson, and La’son led me to revisit my memories of witnessing my mother’s struggle with untreated postpartum psychosis after my sibling’s birth. In this essay, I explore how systemic failures to support both the parent and the child can lead to tragedy, and I argue for a paradigm shift toward family-centered, integrated care. My aim is to challenge the current status quo, highlight the need for early intervention, and advocate for the overlooked voices of people who grow up with parents experiencing psychiatric conditions.

My story

I was one year older than Cora Clancy when my mom developed postpartum psychosis in 1976. She had developed bipolar disorder after my birth; thus, her susceptibility to postpartum psychosis was known to her doctors. Yet it still took two years after my sibling’s birth for adults to recognize how ill she had become. Over decades, I have wondered how it was possible that adults did not know or see what I was seeing continually as a child.

My mother’s symptoms started with suicidal ideation and hearing voices. Under the burden of her emerging illness, she divorced our father and was awarded custody of my brother and me. We lived with her alone as her experiences became more frequent and intense. How could adults not have known that our mom thought she had telepathic powers? How could they not know that she often thought that my brother and I were being killed by Nazis and that she would scream and cry pleading for our lives? Reflecting on recent testimonies of women who experienced postpartum psychosis has helped me reconcile why adults did not know. Over those two years, her symptoms moved from periodic waves of psychosis to the flood of a full-moon tide, so deep that the landscape of her mind was transformed. She would appear completely lucid, then be overtaken by her psychosis, and it was terrifying for her.

The Lindsey Clancy trial testimonies and related public dialogue have put what my mother experienced and what I experienced as a child into clearer perspective. It has also highlighted for me that children who grow up with a parent experiencing psychosis are often invisible in both psychiatric care and public conversations about family tragedy.

Based on what is known today about effective treatments for postpartum psychosis, my mom might have recovered had she received appropriate medical care. Decades of suffering that my mom and family experienced could have unfolded differently.

Fifty years later, in the town of Plymouth, Massachusetts, retrials are pending for two mothers, Lindsey Clancy and Latarsha Sanders, following the deaths of five children: Cora, Dawson, Callan, Edson, and La’son. How many other children and parents have died due to postpartum psychosis or parental mental illness? How many parents with mental illness have been permanently hospitalized or incarcerated in recent years?1 We do not know because we do not collect relevant data.

Postpartum psychosis affects the whole family

Incredible suffering occurs if this medical condition is not recognized and appropriate medical care is not given. Postpartum psychosis occurs at the same rate as other pregnancy complications that are more widely discussed, such as sudden infant death syndrome.2 It is also likely to be underreported. Appropriate care includes not only care for the person but also wider care in how psychiatric professionals interact with and inform families and wider social systems.

In many, if not most, cases, parents who are experiencing mental illnesses of all kinds are loving, intelligent, and attentive caregivers to their children. From my lived experience, I can attest that having a parent who navigates psychiatric treatment can help shape a child into becoming an insightful, caring, and justice-oriented adult. Yet, intentional recognition and support for parents navigating mental health systems is lacking in the United States. Also lacking are informed psychoeducational materials for spouses and extended families, and age-appropriate literature for children.

Numerous countries have laws and medical care systems that provide specialized treatment and support for moms experiencing postpartum psychosis, their children, spouses, and extended families. Most notable are the hospital-based Mom and Baby Units available in the United Kingdom and Australia.

Looking beyond postpartum psychosis specifically, the Australian Emerging Minds/Children of Parents with Mental Illness (COPMI) initiative provides excellent models for supporting parents, their children, spouses, and extended families in a variety of situations where a father or mother is experiencing a mental health condition.

In the United States, there is no national organization that represents people like me who have or had a parent—whether a mother or father—who has psychiatric experiences, including episodic psychosis. As children, we see more and know more than adults realize. This is an uncomfortable truth. Our experiences are distinct and different from adults. We need to engage children and youth about their experiences and learn from them.

In the irreparable context of lives lost, a path forward exists:

  • Early intervention for postpartum psychosis must be substantially improved. Recovery is possible.
  • Children of parents experiencing psychosis should be recognized as people with their own needs for assessment, information, and support.
  • The United States needs integrated, family-centered systems that reject the false choice between protecting children and providing treatment supports for parents.

My mother was not alone. She and other women who experienced postpartum psychosis belong to a historical context in psychiatry. The first known medical documentation of postpartum psychosis in history was recorded by Hippocrates in 400 B.C. The French psychiatrist Louis-Victor Marcé wrote about the “madness of women who are pregnant, recently delivered, or nursing” in 1854.3 Psychiatric patient rights activist Judi Chamberlin was hospitalized in the 1960s because of postpartum psychosis.4 Notable public figures have openly shared that they had a parent who experienced a mental illness, including the feminist icon Gloria Steinem,5 who died one day before the declaration of a mistrial in Lindsey Clancy’s case. Until the late 1970s, women with postpartum psychosis were more likely than not to be placed into state hospitals, disappearing from their children’s lives with no explanation.

Paralysis in our medical system?

Academic debates as to where to place postpartum psychosis in diagnostic manuals may continue, but does this create paralysis in our medical systems leading us to be bystanders?

Testimonies in the Clancy trial are hard to watch, but I urge medical professionals to watch the relevant testimonies of providers, forensic psychiatrists and psychologists, and, to the extent possible, the family members. The trial’s layered content may become a historical record of our systems of care at this moment in time. It may provide ethnographic material for future generations. The trial, news media, social media, and rhetoric have promoted misinformation, discrimination, and stigma. None of this saves the lives of Cora, Dawson, Callan, Edson, and La’son. Yet can this be a tipping point that moves us to reform our laws and to develop proactive medical and public health supports for families? Systemic change should not require a tragedy—yet sometimes it does. We know enough to act. Are we willing to act before another family pays the price?

item.title: The Manosphere: Beyond the Moral Panic
item.description:
Gender

The Manosphere: Beyond the Moral Panic

Why boys and men are drawn to the manosphere and what we can offer instead.

Posted September 14, 2026

Key points
  • The manosphere is a fragmented ecosystem, not a single ideology.
  • Its appeal often begins with real needs for belonging, purpose, status, and self-improvement.
  • Algorithms can turn uncertainty and insecurity into resentment, certainty, and commercial opportunity.
  • Challenging misogyny means offering boys and men healthier ways to become the men they can be.

Perhaps no other issue relating to men has commanded more column inches, news headlines, water-cooler discussions, and political debate in recent times than the manosphere. But what exactly is it, why are people drawn to it, and what can we do about it?

The term is a marriage between man and blogosphere. The manosphere is a mix of often overlapping online communities, including men describing themselves as incels ("involuntary celibates"), pick-up artists (PUAs), Men Going Their Own Way (MGTOW), and men's rights activists (MRAs).

It is tempting to treat these groups as a single, coherent ideology. They aren't. The manosphere is better understood as a fragmented ecosystem: part self-improvement culture, part debate circuit, part social commentary and, at its fringes, extremist. Some of its content is relatively benign; other material is deeply misogynistic, conspiratorial, and destructive.

Why Are Boys and Men Drawn to the Manosphere?

The manosphere foregrounds a model of masculinity that prioritises status, dominance, and sexual prowess. It frequently blames girls and women for the difficulties that boys and men face. In its murkiest corners, it calls for hatred and violence towards them.

Yet if we want to understand its influence, simply condemning the manosphere isn't enough. We need to ask what it is offering.

For many boys and young men, the entry point to the manosphere is self-improvement—a desire to become fitter, wealthier, or more successful. For others, it offers something particularly powerful during adolescence: belonging, certainty, and recognition. Adolescence is a time when people are developing their identities, questioning their place in social hierarchies, taking risks, and yearning for acceptance and respect from peers and the wider adult world. The manosphere speaks to these concerns.

How Manosphere Influencers Draw People in: The B.A.D.G.E.D. Playbook

Drawing on my work with young men and the insights of researchers who have examined the manosphere, I use the acronym B.A.D.G.E.D. to summarise a method consistently employed by some manosphere influencers to enlist and profit from followers:

  • B—Build up the problem: Frame ordinary developmental struggles as personal deficiency. You're not attractive enough. You're not successful enough.
  • A—Attack the mainstream: Position society as deceptive and hostile. You're being misled. Feminism is trying to emasculate you.
  • D—Deliver "hidden" knowledge: Claim to be the voice of truth in a world of lies. You've joined the awakened.
  • G—Gather the tribe: Create a sense of belonging and shared identity. You've joined the awakened.
  • E—Extract payment: Monetise the solution through courses, programmes, subscriptions and investments.
  • D—Drip-feed reminders: Keep the threat alive. Stay sharp. Society will try to trick you.

This approach taps into real concerns experienced by boys and young men: loneliness, uncertainty about identity, pressure to succeed and confusion about relationships. But instead of helping them navigate that complexity, it offers supposed explanations, clear villains, and practical advice. It's the influencers who profit from the subscriptions they acquire and the advertising revenue their social media accounts generate.

Research conducted by Ofcom (2025) found that people who engage with manosphere content don't tend to blindly adhere to everything they encounter. They take what resonates and discard what doesn't. The manosphere is not a conveyor belt leading inexorably to radicalisation. It's closer to a marketplace, with boys and men exercising varying degrees of agency over what they buy into. This distinction matters. Not everyone who engages with the manosphere becomes a "manoslave."

Is he lonely? Curious? Entertained? Learning? Being influenced?
Source: Вальдемар / Pexels

The Real Conspiracy at the Heart of the Manosphere

The manosphere is replete with claims about a "gynaecocracy" of women conspiring to disempower men, feminism deliberately emasculating boys, and women using relationships to benefit their socio-economic standing. I hasten to add that these claims are not supported by any reliable evidence.

Yet conspiracy theories can be psychologically attractive. It can feel safer for some boys and men to believe in a feminist plot against men than to face a life that feels empty of meaning, purpose, and connection. Still, the consequences of these conspiracies can be profound. Misogyny becomes normalised through dehumanising language that eviscerates empathy and compassion and erodes moral constraints on how women and girls are treated.

Violence against women and girls is overwhelmingly perpetrated by men—frequently by current or former intimate partners (World Bank, 2022). We need to be clear about the risks whilst also recognising that not every boy who encounters manosphere content is on a trajectory towards violence. Most men are not violent towards women. The answer cannot simply be to tell boys what not to become. We also need to show them what they can become.

From Prevention to Possibility

The UK government's (2025) strategy on violence against women and girls has highlighted the importance of preventing radicalisation of young men, pursuing abusers, and supporting victims and survivors. Importantly, it also recognises the need to teach young people about manosphere influencers without stigmatising boys. There is a complementary need to support the mental health and wellbeing of boys and men. Preventing radicalisation needs to be coordinated with efforts to foster healthy masculine identities and respect towards women and girls.

We need to offer boys meaningful opportunities to develop skills, take risks, find purpose, contribute to communities, and experience belonging. We need spaces where young men can talk honestly about rejection, loneliness, shame, fear, and uncertainty without being told that vulnerability makes them weak. This is precisely the kind of work that organisations such as Progressive Masculinities are undertaking. Ultimately, we need men to be "upstanders" rather than passive bystanders when misogyny appears in our own social groups. Bad things happen to girls and women when good men say and do nothing.

Become a Smart Scroller

There are steps we can all take in our own interactions with online content. Before liking, sharing or following something, ask:

  1. What is this post trying to make me feel?
  2. Why would the algorithm steer me toward this content?
  3. Who benefits if I react or share this?
  4. What sort of man might I become by engaging with this post?
  5. Would the person I want to be in five years thank me for sharing this content?

What Are We Selling Boys About Being Men?

The manosphere has understood something that we sometimes forget: Boys and young men are searching for answers about what it means to be a man. The question is not whether they will find answers. The question is who will provide them.

We can leave a vacuum and allow influencers to fill it with skewed explanations, resentment, and commercialised insecurity. Or we can offer something better: masculinities built around connection, contribution, care, and purpose.

The real issue isn't men versus women. It's the reward structures that turn misgivings into a marketplace. Manosphere influencers don't just sell ideas; they sell products, lifestyles and, ultimately, a sense of belonging. But the cost can be significant.

Spending time engaging with manosphere content also means that there is less time available to experience offline highs and lows that help us grow as men. Perhaps the challenge isn't simply to take away the "red pill" that is discussed on manosphere forums; it is to offer boys and men something infinitely better—the opportunity to become the compassionate and caring men we can be.

item.title: How to Measure Your Self-Discipline
item.description:
Self-Control

How to Measure Your Self-Discipline

Self-discipline is a quality you can now quantify.

Posted September 14, 2026

Key points
  • Self-discipline is a trainable capacity built in repeated moments of conflict between impulse and intention.
  • What you can measure, you can improve—even for qualities as abstract as self-discipline.
  • A behavioural log of temptations resisted vs given in to can turn acts of self-control into behavioural data.

We all know that self-discipline pushes you toward actions that breed success. It drags us out of bed when we'd rather stay there, gets us to exercise when we’d rather not, and stops us from doing things that feel good now but make our lives worse later.

But how disciplined are you? And what if we could measure that?

The idea of measuring your self-discipline almost sounds unnatural—How can you quantify a quality?

But what if measuring it could help you build it?

First, what is self-discipline?

In The Power of Discipline, Daniel Walter describes self-discipline as the ability to fight against temptations so you can consistently act in your best interests.[1]

Ryan Holiday makes a similar argument in Discipline Is Destiny, describing self-discipline as the ability to avoid the temptations that prevent you from achieving or maintaining success.[2]

According to Walter and Holiday, self-discipline is essentially impulse control—how successfully you resist the urge to do something that might feel good now but does not benefit you once it’s over.[3] And Epictetus agrees:

“It is the part of a wise man to resist pleasures, but of a foolish man to be a slave to them.” [4]

That gives us something we can measure.

Measuring your discipline

Keep a list of the number of temptations you resist vs. give in to. For example:

Source: Dr Manu Sidhu (author)

You could even calculate a self-discipline score:

Temptations resisted ÷ total temptations encountered × 100

While this isn’t a validated psychological measure, it is a personal behavioural measure: a way of making something normally invisible visible.

You could make this score more nuanced by noting how difficult each temptation felt and building that into the formula, but the point isn’t to become obsessive about the number—it’s to leverage the benefits of keeping a physical list:

  • It holds you accountable because what you measure is harder to ignore.
  • The very act of noting down each temptation makes you more conscious of the decision while it is happening.
  • It reveals the impulses you repeatedly struggle to resist so you can come up with better strategies to overcome them.

Instead of asking:

“Am I a disciplined person?”

You start asking:

“Which decisions am I getting better at making?”

That feels much more useful because a disciplined identity is not built all at once. It is constructed through hundreds of individual moments in which what you want now comes into conflict with what you want more.

Even if you never calculate a score, the practice can be reduced to one question whenever that conflict appears:

“Am I going to resist this or give in to it?”

item.title: Grandparenting Is Wonderful; It's Also Complicated
item.description:
Family Dynamics

Grandparenting Is Wonderful; It's Also Complicated

Why emotional complexity is a normal and important part of grandparenting.

Posted September 14, 2026

Key points
  • Mixed feelings are a normal part of loving across generations.
  • Healthy grandparenting makes room for conflicting emotions.
  • Every feeling matters—even those we rarely talk about.

When you became a grandparent, you probably heard some version of the same question:

"Isn't it the best?"

"Don't you just love being a grandparent?"

In my 40 years as a psychologist, I've worked with many grandparents, and I've noticed something striking: Those questions leave very little room for any answer other than an enthusiastic "Absolutely.” There is rarely any space for feelings that don’t fit the cultural narrative that grandparenting is purely joyful.

As a grandparent myself, I understand why. When my older grandson calls my name or runs into my arms, there is no greater joy. However, for many families, becoming a grandparent can also stir up old family wounds, unresolved tensions with adult children, challenges with the physical demands of caring for young children, and sometimes increased financial burdens on grandparents as they help their adult children.

This paradox of being a grandparent is often not discussed, since the only response people feel they can give when talking about it is positive and full of joy. The joy is real. So are the complexities.

So much writing about being a grandparent stays in the “Isn’t this wonderful?” territory. While celebration is important, it often leaves many grandparents feeling isolated when their experiences include frustration, sadness, exhaustion, disappointment, or uncertainty.

Recently, I worked with a new grandmother who is truly struggling with this new role in her life since it’s reopening so many unresolved wounds with her adult daughter. She adores holding and caring for her granddaughter, yet becoming a grandparent has reignited longstanding tensions with her adult daughter. She feels constantly criticized and second-guessed whenever she helps with childcare.

My patient often talks about how she’s ashamed and embarrassed to share her struggles in her new role as grandmother to her friends. Many of her friends spoke about grandparenthood as though it were entirely wonderful, and she worried there was something wrong with her for finding aspects of the role difficult.

There isn’t.

In fact, her experiences reflect something I frequently see in clinical practice: Healthy grandparenting often requires the ability to hold two seemingly contradictory truths simultaneously.

The Power of “And”

Grandparenting can be a wonderful new and exciting role, watching your child become a parent and welcoming a baby to the family, while at the same time, challenges often occur.

The goal is not to resolve the tension between joy and complication but to build the capacity to hold both without collapsing them into one story. This is the paradox for so many people I know about being grandparents.

For so many families with grandparents, I often think of this stage as “holding two truths.” Healthy grandparenting means tolerating emotional complexity.

For example, many grandparents find themselves living in the space of “and.”

  • I adore spending time with my grandchildren...and I miss my independence.
  • I'm proud of my adult child…and I wish they'd take my advice.
  • I'm grateful to babysit...and I'm exhausted.
  • I cherish this role...and sometimes I feel invisible.

Psychologically, this reflects what is often called dialectical thinking: the ability to recognize that two opposing experiences can both be true. It’s not about choosing one feeling over another but, rather, about making room for both.

The Ambivalence Itself Is Normal, Not a Failure

Love and resentment, joy and depletion, connection and need for boundaries can coexist in the same relationship without one canceling the other. Many grandparents (and honestly, many parents) feel they have to pick a side—either "I love this completely" or "I'm struggling"—when, in clinical terms, ambivalence is the more honest response to a complex life transition.

The Hidden Challenges of Grandparenthood

For some grandparents, the challenges are practical as well as emotional.

Some grandparents provide substantial childcare, financial support, or even full-time caregiving. They may be managing their own health concerns, planning for retirement, or having responsibilities to their aging parents.

Other grandparents with whom I have worked struggle to have open access to their grandchildren, as it often depends on maintaining positive relationships with their adult children and partners. Some grandparents may feel that their role is conditional, which leaves them hesitant to express their opinions or to disagree with parenting choices.

Learning to Love While Letting Go

Perhaps the greatest psychological task of grandparenting isn’t learning how to love our grandchildren—we usually do that effortlessly.

It’s learning to love while letting go.

Letting go of being the primary decision-maker—even when you might be providing much of the childcare.

Letting go of always having the answers.

Letting go of the expectation that this chapter of life will look exactly as we had imagined.

Grandparenting often requires a delicate balance: remaining deeply connected while accepting that the next generation is now in charge.

Every Feeling Matters

We often teach young children that having “mixed” feelings is OK. A child can be excited and nervous, happy and sad, confident and scared—all at once. I hope that many grandparents allow themselves to have these mixed feelings too, since being a grandparent, of course, can be joyous but can also stimulate other, sometimes opposing feelings.

I remember reading a book to my almost 3-year-old grandson about how all feelings matter—and hopefully the same can be true for grandparents.

Joy and exhaustion.

Pride and disappointment.

Connection and longing.

These aren’t contradictions—they’re all part of being human.

The healthiest grandparenting may not come from pretending the difficult feelings don’t exist but from making room for all of them.

As I read this book about feelings to my 3-year-old grandson, I'm reminded of a truth that applies to all of us: Every feeling matters—even ours!

item.title: The More Time I Spend in Nature, the Kinder I Become
item.description:
Environment

The More Time I Spend in Nature, the Kinder I Become

Personal Perspective: Time outdoors builds perspective, patience, and compassion.

Posted September 14, 2026

Key points
  • Time in nature can create space between a stressful event and your response.
  • Perspective from the outdoors can make everyday frustrations feel more manageable.
  • Daily outdoor time can strengthen patience, humility, and care for others.

I spend a lot of time seeking out places where there’s no cell service, no traffic, no televisions, no people, and very little that resembles the world I normally live in. Instead, mine is filled with remote mountains, high altitude, wind, snow, rivers, and, sometimes, weather so severe that finding shelter becomes the priority.

One of the things I’m learning is that the longer I spend in nature, the more patient I seem to become with people when I return home.

That sounds almost too simple, but I notice it again and again after each expedition. Someone yells at me, and I’m more likely to let it go. A car cuts me off in traffic, and instead of getting angry, I might laugh. A potential client doesn't return my phone call, and I’m less likely to make up a story about what it means or take it personally.

I don't suddenly become a saint. I still get irritated and have bad days. There’s a good reason why I meditate daily. But the amount of space between what another person does and how I respond is different.

Gaining Perspective

I think nature gives us more room. When I spend enough time outdoors, especially in places vast enough to humble me, my own problems begin to feel more manageable.

On an expedition, I worry about what matters most in the moment: finding a safe route, getting enough water, protecting my hands from the cold, deciding whether conditions are safe enough to continue. But then I look up, and there’s a mountain in front of me that’s been there for thousands, perhaps millions, of years. The wind moves across it. Clouds form and disappear. Nature becomes a breathing, living entity, and I'm fortunate enough to witness and be a part of it.

The more time I spend outside, the more I carry that feeling of wholeness home. Nature slows me down. It gives me perspective. And that perspective follows me into ordinary moments of my day, including the moments when another person does something that would normally get under my skin. I can't prove that a mountain can make you a kinder person; I just know what happens to me.

I find the connection between those two things fascinating.

Environmental Compassion

People talk about environmental compassion. We teach one another to recycle, protect forests, care about wildlife, and reduce pollution. Those things matter, of course, but are we also missing something else? I think learning to care about the natural world can help us practice caring more about one another.

When I’m outside, I’m reminded that I’m part of something I cannot control. Nature doesn't care about my schedule. It doesn't care whether I am having a good day. A storm doesn't change its mind because I’m frustrated. That is humbling. And humility can be useful when dealing with other people.

The person who cuts you off in traffic may be having a terrible day. Someone who doesn't call you back may be overwhelmed. Your colleague who snaps at you may be carrying something you know nothing about.

You don't have to excuse bad behavior. Compassion doesn't mean allowing people to treat you poorly. It means creating enough distance between their behavior and your reaction that you can choose what to do next.

I find nature helps me create that distance.

So, I have a simple prescription I’d like to pass along. Try to spend at least 30 minutes to an hour outside every day. Plant something in your garden. Walk around your neighborhood. Sit on a park bench or in the grass. Take a hike. Walk the dog. Eat lunch outdoors. Sit under a tree and leave your phone in your pocket.

The activity isn't nearly as important as the contact. Give yourself enough time to notice what is around you. Over time, you may find yourself becoming slower to anger, more patient in traffic, and less likely to assume the worst when someone disappoints you.

I think as we become better at caring for the world around us, we’ll become better at caring for the people in it. That is certainly what continues to happen for me.

item.title: The Good News About Nightmares
item.description:
Dreaming

The Good News About Nightmares

A review and discussion of "The Dream Hotel" by Laila Lalami.

Posted September 14, 2026

Key points
  • Nightmares and bad dreams are fairly common.
  • Dreams bring emotions to the forefront for processing.
  • Dreamscapes provide a way of problem-solving and learning waking time strategies.
Source: Alex Pavor / Unsplash

Sara Hussein, an archivist for the Getty Museum, returns home from a conference in London and is pulled aside at passport control. The reason? Her security “risk score” is too high.

Thus begins the dystopian plot of the book, The Dream Hotel, by Laila Lalami. Lalami paints a world where an artificial intelligence (AI) algorithm routinely flags citizens for their potential to commit a crime using a government-endorsed online surveillance system. Everyone is monitored closely for “future intent,” their behavior scrutinized at every turn. Even dreams are monitored and flagged for content, having been recorded and reviewed thanks to a neural implant designed to correct sleep apnea. Because of her dreams, the book’s protagonist is considered at high risk for violence and is arrested at the airport.

Setting aside the other societal themes this book explores, The Dream Hotel raises an important question: How are we to understand disturbing emotions and experiences we have when we’re asleep?

Getting a Good Night’s Sleep

I don’t know anyone who hasn’t been angry with their partner at something. Or at the dog. Or at traffic. Face it—we humans tend to get upset, whether we show it or not. And these emotions find their way into our dreams.

In one dream, Sara is on a hike with her husband and, in a moment of annoyance, swats the camera from his hand, only to watch him plunge off a bridge into a churning river below. Instead of helping him, she freezes. She’s horrified, both in the dream and upon waking. Sure, she was annoyed at him in the dream when she swatted the camera. But then, instead of helping, she froze. Does this make her a potential criminal in waking life?

Let’s talk about nightmares. The first word that comes to mind is usually fear, but nightmares also include anger, anxiety, and grief. Sometimes they are intense enough to wake us up, but plenty of times they do not, leading researchers Zadra and Donderi (2000) to look at nightmares and bad dreams as two different categories. In their studies, nightmares and bad dreams are relatively common. In one four-week trial, they found that 83 percent of participants reported at least one nightmare or bad dream during that time.

Nightmares, bad dreams, and good dreams are part of our internal regulating system. In one review, Perogamvros and researchers (2013) found dreams activate our emotion and reward circuits, suggesting that when we dream, we play out scenarios, allowing us to process memories and emotions and learn new behaviors. This nighttime dreaming “work” is associated with improved waking time feelings of well-being, better social skills, and creativity.

In another review, Scarpelli and team (2019) highlight that the memories utilized in dreams are often part of a created dream scenario, not necessarily a literal re-telling. Revonsuo (2000) suggests in the threat-simulation hypothesis that these semi-fabricated dream scenarios provide a “virtual world” for problem-solving and learning new emotional strategies in the safe spaces of sleep.

Let’s turn again to our fictional dreamer, Sara. In the book, Sara analyzes her own dream. In the dream, she was annoyed that her husband was rushing her along the trail. She remembers wanting to take in the view instead, to feel the moss on the rocks. Connecting her dream to waking life, she realized that this dream occurred at a pivotal point in their relationship, when he wanted kids, and she wasn’t ready. The dream signaled the disconnect between what each of them wanted for their lives. Swatting the camera was her dismissing her husband’s view; freezing was her pattern when faced with conflict.

According to real-life research, our character’s analysis tracks. Playing out a charged emotional scenario in the dreamscape helps us to process emotions, and gives us a window into how we are reacting to challenges, so that we can respond differently in waking time. Well done, Sara!

The Dream Journal

The longer the character of Sara is kept in detention, the more insistent she becomes in trying to understand the data points that the algorithm used to flag her as a potentially violent threat. She begins to keep a dream journal to capture the content of her dreams. Keeping this journal becomes her greatest comfort, allowing her to access deeper aspects of herself that she had previously ignored. It’s through this reflection that she captures her thoughts around the hiking dream that so troubled her and led to her arrest.

In the real world, as with this character, keeping a dream journal has been shown in multiple studies to help us to not only remember our dreams but also to better understand ourselves. Baikie & Wilhelm (2005) found that journaling can facilitate emotional processing and contribute to an overall enhanced well-being. As in the case of our protagonist, journaling about our dreams and emotions can help us better understand the challenges we face and help us to bring them to resolution.

Most everyone I’ve ever spoken with has remembered an unpleasant dream in their life. Much of the time we want to get away from the feeling as fast as we can. But dreamscapes can help us problem-solve in waking life with images that can serve as grist for introspection. In other words, you might sense you aren’t on the same page as your partner, but having a nightmare about seeing him plunge off a bridge might highlight the issue that can be addressed… and resolved.

Luckily, none of us live in a Dream Hotel, but all of us dream. Rather than signaling a potential crime, as depicted in the dystopian novel, our dreams may be simply signaling a potential concern as part of our well-being toolkit.

Gratitude to Lalami for bringing dreams to the forefront in the thought-provoking and fantastic read of The Dream Hotel.

item.title: Winning the Conversation, Losing the Connection
item.description:
Relationships

Winning the Conversation, Losing the Connection

Why some couples talk over each other instead of talking with each other.

Posted September 14, 2026

Key points
  • Competing to talk often prevents partners from truly listening.
  • 'Pause' and 'Accountability' help couples recognize how both partners contribute to escalation.
  • Repair begins when understanding and listening become more important than impressing and winning.
Source: kokimk/123rf.com

Nina and Eric often joked that they could talk about anything. Friends admired their energy, intelligence, and quick wit. Both were successful professionals who enjoyed lively conversations and shared a genuine curiosity about the world. Early in their relationship, their spirited debates felt exciting and sexy. They challenged each other's ideas, laughed often, and appreciated having a partner who could keep up intellectually.

Over time, however, those conversations began to change. What once felt engaging and compelling gradually became a source of frustration. They felt the growing tension but kept up their conversational intensity because talking about anything and everything had become part of their identity as a couple. The problem was that they had started listening less and competing more.

When considering what we call the Four Pillars of True Love—vulnerability, empathy, intimacy, and emotional investment—they might have given themselves, and each other, high marks. But when they actually slowed down and reflected on themselves (Pause), they realized they did not know how to be vulnerable with each other.

They discovered that their intellectual connection and passion were covering up insecurity and vulnerability. Neither knew how to say something as simple as, “Can we just chill this weekend without doing something intellectually stimulating or engaging?” Questions like these felt surprisingly vulnerable. The more insecure they felt, the more they relied on intellectual conversation. Gradually, the intensity and competitiveness of their conversations escalated into a zero-sum game of winning or losing.

Crash: When Every Conversation Becomes an Attempt to Impress

The pattern appeared most often during disagreements but eventually spread into ordinary conversations. If Nina interrupted, it was because she feared losing her train of thought. If Eric raised his voice, it was because he felt he had already been interrupted three times. Each believed the other was controlling the conversation while viewing their own behavior as a necessary response.

A discussion about finances quickly became an argument about whose financial ideas were better. A conversation about weekend plans shifted into competing explanations about whose ideas were more romantic. Before long, both were talking at once, each trying harder to make a point while becoming less aware of what the other was actually saying. Ironically, the harder they fought to be heard, the less heard either of them felt. The intellectual conversations that once bonded them were now seriously disrupting their relationship.

In our book, Love. Crash. Rebuild., we describe rupture as the moment partners stop experiencing themselves as collaborators and begin responding to each other as opponents. Once that shift occurs, even small disagreements can escalate because both partners are protecting themselves rather than remaining open and curious about each other.

Rebuild: Using PACER to Slow the Conversation

Pause

In therapy, Eric and Nina agreed to pause and commit to three things:

  1. Hit pause when feeling agitated or competitive.
  2. Stop filling awkward silences.
  3. Take a deliberate, deep breath before jumping into a conversation to curb impulsive overtalking.

The turning point came when Nina noticed that neither of them could accurately summarize what the other had just said. She realized she had been so busy forming her own response (reaction) that she was no longer listening to Eric's actual words.

Pause interrupted their momentum. Instead of continuing to argue, Nina asked a simple question: “Are we trying to understand each other and connect, or are we trying to win?”

Eric looked startled and responded, “I think I was trying to win. I wasn't trying to have a conversation.”

Accountability

Eric acknowledged that he was also busy forming his own thoughts because he feared his perspective would never be fully heard. He wanted to keep up with Nina's quick wit.

Nina acknowledged that she frequently finished Eric's sentences because she wanted to show him how smart she was. She worried that Eric might not like her as much if she could not keep up or offer ideas of her own. Impressing him helped her feel accepted and admired.

Being intellectual conversationalists was certainly part of their identity, but they realized they had also been using that identity to impress each other and cover up their insecurities.

Collaboration

Together, they agreed that understanding would become more important than responding quickly. They practiced allowing each other to finish speaking before offering a reply.

They also discovered that summarizing what they had heard before responding slowed the conversation enough for empathy to reappear.

Experiment

For several weeks, they tried one simple rule: Whoever was listening had to summarize what they had heard before sharing their own perspective.

The conversations initially felt awkward, but gradually became calmer. Neither partner felt the same urgency to compete for the floor because each knew there would be an opportunity to speak.

Reset

Their disagreements did not disappear, but they stopped being so exhausting. Instead of leaving conversations feeling frustrated, defeated, or misunderstood, both partners increasingly felt heard—even when they continued to disagree.

Their relationship became quieter, not because they cared less, but because they no longer experienced every conversation as something one person had to win.

Why This Matters

Many couples believe communication problems are caused by their partner. More often, problems develop because neither partner can stop talking long enough to listen. Constant talking can also cover up both partners' insecurities.

The PACER process helps couples slow emotional escalation, increase accountability, and create conversations that foster understanding rather than competition. The goal of a difficult conversation is not to win the argument. It is to understand and connect with each other.
