item.title: The Executive Binge: Alcohol, Cocaine, and Sex
item.description:
Addiction

The Executive Binge: Alcohol, Cocaine, and Sex

How alcohol can trigger a hidden cycle of cocaine, sex, binges, and remorse.

Posted September 14, 2026

Key points
  • Alcohol is often the “permission giver" that lowers inhibitions and opens the door to a cocaine and sex binge.
  • Cocaine can have powerful aphrodisiac effects that reinforce a compulsive cocaine-sex connection.
  • Early treatment must focus on interrupting the “setups” that precede the alcohol-cocaine-sex binge cycle.

A familiar but newly resurfaced pattern among high-functioning men starts with business drinking that turns into marathon episodes of cocaine use, sexual escapades, disappearance, and remorse.

Over the past two years or so, I’ve seen a striking increase in the number of high-functioning men in my private practice struggling with a binge pattern I once saw routinely. It was commonplace among patients I treated during the cocaine epidemic of the 1980s (Washton, 1989a), but in the intervening three decades had become relatively uncommon.

The pattern is intermittent rather than continuous, but when it occurs it is often dramatic. A business dinner or night out with coworkers and other professional associates begins with heavy drinking. Cocaine enters the picture, sometimes right at the restaurant or bar, and the evening becomes a marathon binge of alcohol, cocaine, and sex, often moving to a strip club and then a hotel room with escorts until the next morning or beyond. What follows is also familiar. Calls and texts from spouses go unanswered. The person goes “radio silent,” then resurfaces exhausted and riddled with shame, anxiety, and remorse.

Seeing this pattern reappear after so many years creates a powerful sense of déjà vu. In the early to mid-1980s, I was among a relatively small group of addiction specialists calling attention to a rapidly growing but largely hidden cocaine problem among middle- and upper-income Americans (Washton, Gold, & Pottash, 1984). Cocaine was at that time widely regarded as relatively benign and nonaddictive, yet those seeking my help described patterns of compulsive out-of-control use causing serious psychological, relationship, financial, and occupational consequences. I later described this problem and its treatment in my first book on cocaine addiction (Washton, 1989b).

“But This Only Happens Occasionally”

These men usually are not using cocaine daily or even weekly. They may go weeks or months between episodes with little desire for cocaine in between, making the pattern easy to minimize or dismiss as a “problem,” let alone an “addiction.” The salient issue is not how often this happens, but what happens once it starts. If sporadic use repeatedly produces prolonged binges, deception, sexual risk-taking, disappearance, or relationship damage, infrequency should not be confused with control.

Alcohol Is Often the “Permission Giver”

For many, cocaine is not where the cycle begins. Alcohol removes inhibitions and opens the door. It is the “permission giver.” When not intoxicated, these men may have no intention of obtaining cocaine or pursuing paid sex. After several drinks, judgment changes, inhibitions dissolve, and cocaine suddenly seems like a good idea.

Cocaine and Sex Can Become a Powerful Pairing

Research and clinical experience show that cocaine and other stimulants have strong aphrodisiac effects in a significant number of male users (Rawson et. al., 2002). It can intensify sexual arousal, fantasies, preoccupation, and disinhibition, sometimes fueling hypersexuality and a wide range of sexual acting out behaviors. Cocaine and sex can become tightly paired, each reinforcing the other. Sexual cues may trigger cocaine use, just as cocaine may trigger hypersexuality. Treatment needs to assess this connection directly.

“Do I Have to Stop Drinking Completely?”

A common question is: “Do I have to give up alcohol completely to quit cocaine? My goal is to become a social drinker without having it lead to cocaine and everything else that follows.” Treatment should determine whether drinking actually can be separated from cocaine use. For some, carefully defined limits may prove workable. For others, alcohol is such a powerful gateway that abstaining is safer and easier. A period without alcohol can help break the alcohol-cocaine-sex connection and permit a more realistic evaluation later of whether moderate drinking is feasible.

Recognizing the “Setups”

A key task in early treatment is to identify the “setups” for the next binge (Washton & Zweben, 2009). The binge does not start when cocaine appears. It may begin days earlier with an upcoming business trip, dinner with a particular client, reconnecting with certain colleagues, or deciding, “I’ll go out, but this time I’ll keep it under control.” Mapping the overt and covert events that preceded earlier binges helps identify the earliest links in the chain and short-circuit the process before momentum takes over.

When Partying Is Part of the Job

Breaking this pattern can be especially difficult when coworkers, supervisors, or clients are involved. As discussed in my earlier Psychology Today post, “Executive Binge Drinking: When the ‘Off Switch’ Disappears,” executive roles and corporate cultures can facilitate heavy drinking and conceal its consequences. Drinking, cocaine, strip clubs, and paid sex may become intertwined with client cultivation and male bonding: “This isn’t just partying. It’s part of doing business.” Refusing to participate may feel as though it could jeopardize a client relationship, job status, or acceptance by influential colleagues. Treatment must address these realities rather than simply advising someone to “avoid triggers.”

Confidentiality Matters

For executives, physicians, attorneys, financial professionals, and others with visible careers, fear of exposure can deter treatment. Discreet, confidential outpatient care can offer a practical alternative to more disruptive treatment while allowing people to continue working and meeting family responsibilities.

Good Prognosis

The good news is that this pattern can change. Prognosis is often quite good when high-functioning people are willing to make necessary changes: leaving events earlier, declining invitations, avoiding certain people or venues, or finding new ways to entertain clients. In many cases, abstaining from alcohol, at least temporarily, greatly improves the chances of breaking the pattern. People who have a history of succeeding in demanding areas of life often bring useful strengths to treatment: persistence, problem-solving ability, discipline, and the capacity to make difficult decisions when they understand what is at stake. With appropriate help and sustained effort, breaking the alcohol-cocaine-sex cycle is an achievable goal.

item.title: Perfectionism: Protection or Prison?
item.description:
Perfectionism

Perfectionism: Protection or Prison?

Seeming in perfect control can feel safe while also being its own private hell.

Posted September 14, 2026

Key points
  • Creating a highly successful, perfect-seeming life can also serve as distraction from or camouflage for pain.
  • The compartmentalization of emotions that can't be experienced in a certain moment is healthy skill.
  • It can however easily become rigidly protective and create a fear of emotional transparency or vulnerability.

When a child or young adult experiences their world as unsafe, full of conflict or trauma, harshly governed by exacting parents, or empty of any measure of emotional security, they can escape through working toward a world where safety is discovered in accomplishment. Constant accomplishment. Seeming perfect, being the highest achiever while in tight emotional control, may create an effective and intricate camouflage.

The camouflage you wear every day keeps you undetected. That's its purpose. You can go about your life without anyone knowing what you're truly feeling—and that can feel very safe.

Yet despair and loneliness can lie underneath, silently growing more potent. And the camouflage that hides you can become its own prison. You must constantly guard against any pain from showing or escaping. It's not that the pain isn't there. It's there all right. But it's shoved behind locked doors in the shadows of your mind while you then stand guard outside, so that no person can see past the perfection that you seem to portray.

I've called this perfectly hidden depression; it has 10 telltale traits that keep it solidly in place. Yet those traits can also be either kept or challenged.

From compartmentalization to emotional rigidity

You might ask yourself, Do I want to feel this feeling right now? Is it safe to do so? If the answer is no, your mind suppresses that feeling, deliberately changing your focus.

Here's an example.

If your beloved dog died one morning, but you had a class to teach, you’d suppress your sadness. You’d decide, “I just can’t think (or feel) about that right now.” The same would happen if you’d won the lottery. Good or bad, you’d put it away.

Another name for suppression is compartmentalization, a concept that might be easier to imagine. It’s like boxing something up. When you compartmentalize a memory or emotion, you put it away in a box and stow it away, not focusing on it or giving it attention.

Here’s the irony. The compartmentalization of emotional pain—the protective armor of saying “I’m fine” or “I’ve got this”—may have become an identity that you now feel you cannot escape. This perfectionistic camouflage that initially served as protection can become its own kind of prison.

What this looks like in contrast to what it feels like

So, what does someone with perfectly hidden depression look like to the outside world? From the “outside in,” you appear successful and happy. You’re the highly successful (and compassionate) divorce lawyer. The boss who knows everyone’s birthday and also leads with integrity. The community volunteer who can get things done.

You’re known for your intelligence, caring, and leadership.

But from the “inside out,” you feel constant pressure, even fear.

Thus, it can become vital to guard that prison diligently, both from within—where you can’t allow painful emotions to resurface—and from without, where you remain hyper-vigilant, fearing someone might guess your secret struggle. You must do double duty so that no one can see that your prison even exists. You’re both prisoner and guard simultaneously. And you’ll go to great lengths to prevent anyone from figuring that out.

This pattern can become so much of who you understand yourself to be that you may not realize exactly what you’re doing, feeling, or better yet…not feeling.

And there can be immense cost to this constant pressure.

You may identify with Chelsea

Chelsea came in to see me because she’d watched my TEDx on perfectly hidden depression. “I don’t know what even made me watch it. It was something about the ‘perfectly hidden’ part,” she said. Then she laughed sarcastically. “I have so many secrets I’m not sure where to start. Or if I can really do this at all.”

When I asked her if she felt any fear, she simply stated, “I’m afraid all of who I am will fall apart. It’s like pulling on a loose thread on a sweater. Pretty soon, the whole thing will be ripped up and unwearable.”

She said this to me matter-of-factly, without any emotion.

Yet, you can hear Chelsea's fear. It was palpable in the room as she spoke.

There's a way to not unravel. There's a way to begin to identify what's positive about your strivings to be successful and "put-together," while at the same time realizing that there are pieces of that camouflage that you might begin to see as not helpful.

And slowly risk opening a small window and allowing yourself the freedom to breathe without hiding.

item.title: In Gaming, Where Are the Parents?
item.description:
Parenting

In Gaming, Where Are the Parents?

Blaming parents for harms in online video games misses the point.

Posted September 14, 2026

Key points
  • Many people online blame parents when their children are harmed by strangers on Roblox.
  • Despite harms that occur on the platform, Roblox presents itself as safe for children.
  • Many good parents trust platforms like Roblox and unwittingly expose their children to harm.

Last month, a bipartisan group of senators launched an investigation into Roblox for failing to protect the minors who use its platforms from child predators. I've written previously about some of the specific ways Roblox is dangerous for minors and how parents can work to protect their children.

Briefly, Roblox facilitates communication between players, some of whom have bad intentions. Roblox has been sued dozens of times for children being sexually or otherwise physically harmed by people who met them on the platform. They also allow any user to create their own games, many of which are highly inappropriate for children. Their moderation team is insufficient to keep up with millions of users, comments, and games. Many of the moderators of these games are minors themselves.

In the comment section under every article about these harms, someone parrots the same talking point: “Where are the parents? It’s not Roblox’s fault that these irresponsible parents let their children get hurt.”

Of course parents bear responsibility for their children’s safety, but blaming them is misguided.

Roblox promises that it prioritizes child safety and has a reassuring list of steps it has taken to make the games as safe as possible, “partner[ing] with law enforcement, mental health professionals, and global safety experts to guide [its] policies, products, systems, and roadmaps.”

In interviews, they stress that their goal is to make Roblox “the safest platform on the internet” and list a number of reasons parents can feel reassured that their children are safe. It’s easy to imagine a caring but exhausted parent looking at these promises after a long day at work and taking Roblox’s words at face value.

Over a third of parents don’t use any of the safety controls on the platform, presumably trusting that a game company that claims to prioritize safety would create a safe online space for kids. Almost a fourth of Millennial parents aren’t even aware that parental controls exist in Roblox. (I recommend that parents enable parental controls, review the available options, and disable communication from strangers.)

I can imagine several reasons that good parents could make choices that would expose their children to harm. For example:

  1. Some parents probably know that the game is popular with their child’s friends and classmates, think to themselves, “It’s just a game, how bad could it be?” and let their kid play. They never find out that the game allows strangers to talk to their children.

  2. Others are more wary and do some more research. They go to Roblox’s website, click “Safety Center,” and read that Roblox takes content moderation seriously, that they partner with law enforcement and use sophisticated systems to make sure that all inappropriate content is restricted, and are reassured. They never learn that the moderation system is woefully insufficient.

    Why would someone who believes Roblox’s talking points look for ways to make their children’s experience safer?

  3. Even when parents are involved, know to be careful, and set appropriate parental controls, it’s still too easy to circumvent them. Signing up for a fresh Roblox account with no restrictions takes less than a minute and doesn’t even require an email address. Their new age verification system is laughably easy to get around.

That’s why I wrote a book explaining video games to parents, because many parents don’t know about issues like this. They can’t protect their children against threats they don’t know to watch for.

Ultimately, parents are responsible for their children’s well-being. However, they can only protect against threats they know about. Roblox and other games and platforms have a moral obligation to protect children. As they have proven unwilling to take reasonable steps to do so, I believe it is our collective responsibility to force them to. I’m glad that lawmakers are starting to take this seriously.

item.title: Bonds and Biology: How Social Media Engages Reward Systems
item.description:
Social Media

Bonds and Biology: How Social Media Engages Reward Systems

Why social media does not impact oxytocin in the same ways as real connections.

Posted September 14, 2026

Key points
  • Social media can trigger dopamine-driven validation.
  • Oxytocin release via digital interaction lacks the rich multisensory cues of face-to-face contact.
  • Likes and notifications can create reward cycles that differ from genuine social support or bonding.

Social media has altered how many people connect, communicate, and maintain relationships. Yet questions remain around what happens to biological systems, evolved for real face-to-face relationships, when they are activated through screens. Important for this discussion is oxytocin, a neuropeptide associated with social bonding, trust, and attachment1. While oxytocin is directly involved with social connection, it is also activated by the dopamine systems involved in social validation (and/or reward)2. The dissociation between social connection (involving oxytocin1,3) and social validation (involving dopamine2) may underlie a problem with assuming that digital networks are truly social. Social media can engage some of the biological pathways related to social validation and social reward that are also connected with the experience of real-world relationships1,4. Such social validation triggers dopamine, which, in turn, can facilitate oxytocin release. However, the nature and consequences of these indirect oxytocin activations, through social validation, differ from its release resulting from direct social connections, and any resulting confusion can have negative impacts on well-being1,3,4.

Environmental pressures have favoured development of a degree of social interaction for some species, and the brains of many ‘social’ species contain specialised systems to process social cues, evaluate social rewards, and, through these processes, maintain relationships4. The amygdala, prefrontal cortex, mentalising network, and reward systems of mammals all contribute to the formation and maintenance of social connections1. Oxytocin and its receptor genes are involved in the experience of social affiliation, trust, empathy, information sharing, and social network size and quality1,3. Individuals with stronger activity in these systems, and with more active/impactful oxytocin, often maintain larger and more complex social networks1,4,5.

How Social Media Engages Biological Reward Pathways

Social media can provide rewarding stimuli associated with social bonding4, such as likes, positive comments, and recognition from others, that can act as digital analogues of social reward3. These engage biological systems, including dopamine-mediated pathways, associated with reinforcement learning4. These pathways are important for social bonding to occur, as if the social interaction is not positive, why continue with it? Thus, social reward is important in facilitating social life1,3, and it indirectly facilitates oxytocin. This oxytocin can make people feel as if there is social connection or bonding, especially in the absence of other social cues important for telling them whether interactions are true or fake. These extra cues are missing in digital media, and their absence makes it easier to use digital social validation nefariously to trick people into believing that there is a real connection. However, reward-connected validation systems are not synonymous with systems involved in real-world social connection1,4. Consequently, social media may stimulate social-reward systems, but does not necessarily produce social connection associated with oxytocin and offline relationships1,4.

In fact, social media lacks several critical features of face-to-face interactions. Real-world relationships involve rich multisensory experiences: eye contact, facial expressions, vocal tone, touch, smell, and synchronised behaviour, which influence oxytocin systems1,3. Real-world interactions often involve physical proximity and touch, two of the strongest natural triggers of bonding and oxytocin. Parent-child contact, affectionate touch between partners, and face-to-face emotional communication, are consistently linked with stronger oxytocin-related responses than abstract social engagement1,3. By contrast, social media interactions are often brief, asynchronous, highly curated, devoid of physical contact, and reduced to simplified social signals. A thumbs-up or heart emoji may signal social approval (validation), but do not reproduce the full biological context of sitting with a friend, hugging a partner, or comforting a child1,4.

In a healthy and consistent environment, oxytocin may help reinforce meaningful relationships that promote well-being and social support. Online platforms, however, can create highly concentrated streams of social rewards that are unpredictable and intermittent3. Notifications, comments, likes, and follower counts function to produce random ratio schedules of reward (where reinforcement follows varying and unpredictable numbers of responses), a mechanism known to strongly promote high levels of behaviour3. The result may be a situation where users repeatedly seek social validation through digital interactions. Rather than strengthening genuine social bonds, individuals can become preoccupied with monitoring their online presence, chasing validation, or fearing social exclusion. This validation-chasing makes them even more vulnerable to social predators.

Why Distinguishing Connection from Validation Matters

This distinction between connection and validation is crucial. Oxytocin evolved to facilitate relationships and social cohesion, but social media platforms sometimes redirect those basic biological tendencies toward engagement metrics (social reward), rather than meaningful human relationships (social connection). One explanation, noted above, is that digital interactions may only partially satisfy underlying social needs. Someone may accumulate hundreds of online interactions, yet still experience loneliness if those interactions lack emotional depth or reciprocal support3,4.

In contrast, real-world social networks are strongly associated with better well-being, increased perceived social support, lower rates of depression and anxiety, and even improved physical health outcomes1. Thus, while social media can expand social reach, it may not fully replicate the protective benefits associated with close, embodied, real-world relationships.

In conclusion, the evidence suggests that social media engages some of the same biological systems as are involved in human bonding, including reward pathways and potentially oxytocin-related mechanisms. However, digital interactions appear to provide only a partial substitute for the multisensory, emotionally rich experiences that characterise face-to-face relationships1,3,4. Used well, social media can support existing relationships, facilitate community building, and provide valuable social support. Used excessively or compulsively, it may exploit (or subvert) the social-reward systems that evolved to foster healthy human connection, contributing to patterns of dependence, and reduced well-being1,4. The challenges for modern society are to understand the biological effects of social media, and to recognise that a notification, however rewarding, is not the same as genuine human presence.
